articles.title: In 1941, Michigan bottler John Makinen built a house from 60,000 chipped and flawed bottles discarded by his soda factory; in 1983, the local historical society bought it for a museum
articles.summary: What began as a practical way to make use of unwanted glass bottles eventually became one of Michigan's most unusual historic buildings.
articles.body: What began as a practical way to make use of unwanted glass bottles eventually became one of Michigan's most unusual historic buildings. In 1941, Kaleva businessman John Makinen built a house using about 60,000 glass bottles that had been chipped or otherwise deemed unsuitable at his local pop bottling factory. According to the Kaleva Historical Society, Makinen arranged the bottles in different colours and patterns, turning what might otherwise have been factory waste into a distinctive home. More than four decades later, in 1983, the Kaleva Historical Society purchased the property with help from community fundraising and turned it into the home of its museum.A house made from unwanted bottlesThe Bottle House stands in the small Michigan community of Kaleva, where its unusual exterior remains difficult to miss. Makinen owned the local pop bottling factory, and the bottles used in the house came from his own business. Rather than allowing chipped or flawed bottles to go to waste, he found another use for them.Around 60,000 glass bottles eventually became part of the house. They were incorporated into the walls with their bottoms facing outward, creating an exterior made up of thousands of individual pieces of coloured glass. Different bottle shapes and colours were arranged in patterns, giving the building an appearance unlike an ordinary brick or wooden house. The design was not simply a matter of putting bottles wherever they would fit. The arrangement of the different colours became part of the building's visual character, and the house became a curiosity for people visiting Kaleva.John Makinen's unusual ideaMakinen was a Finnish immigrant who had become part of the community after moving to the area in the early 20th century. He operated the Northwestern Bottling Works in Kaleva and was involved in local business life. According to the historical accounts of the building, Makinen used surplus bottles from the bottling operation to construct the house. The bottles were laid horizontally, with their bottoms facing the outside. This allowed the colourful glass bases to become a visible part of the walls.Architectural records describe the building as a one-and-a-half-storey bungalow with bottle-filled exterior walls. Different types of bottles were used, including bottles in several shapes and colours, adding decorative patterns to the structure. The result was both a home and an example of resourcefulness. Materials that had lost their original purpose at a bottling plant were given a completely different role in the construction of a house.The bottle house became a local attractionThe building attracted attention even before it became a museum. The Kaleva Historical Society says the unusual house was already a tourist draw because of its distinctive construction and colourful bottle walls. That attention eventually helped give the building a second life.By the early 1980s, the property was available for purchase. Members of the Kaleva Historical Society saw an opportunity to preserve the unusual structure while also giving the community's growing collection of historical objects a permanent home. The society raised money within the community and purchased the property from the Makinen family in 1983. The building subsequently became the society's permanent museum home.From unusual home to history museumToday, the Bottle House is much more than a building made from glass. The museum contains exhibits documenting the history of Kaleva and the people who settled there. Much of that material focuses on the area's Finnish-American heritage, local businesses, farming and the lives of early residents.Visitors can also explore family histories and old photographs, with the collection offering a chance for people with connections to the area to look for relatives, former homes and other pieces of their family history. Other exhibits cover subjects including Kaleva's early businesses, its school, the local bank robbery, community murals and the area's veterans. The building itself is therefore part of the museum's collection. Walking through it means seeing the history of the community while standing inside the unusual structure that helped preserve it.The Makinen name lives on at the museumThe museum also has a dedicated exhibit connected to the Makinen name. The Makinen Tackle Room, which opened in 2009, showcases the history of the Makinen Tackle Company. The company began in Kaleva in the 1940s and eventually produced large numbers of fishing lures and other products.The collection includes examples of the lures made by the company, along with Mak-Kraft decorative items and other objects connected with the business. This gives visitors another connection to the local businesses and families that helped shape Kaleva.A piece of Finnish-American historyThe Bottle House also sits within a community whose identity is closely connected to Finnish immigration. Kaleva was established by Finnish immigrants around the beginning of the 20th century, and the village itself was named after the Finnish epic Kalevala. The historical society has preserved many aspects of that heritage through its museum collections and other community projects.The museum's exhibits include material on early settlers, farming and community life, helping place Makinen's unusual house within the larger story of Kaleva rather than treating it simply as an architectural curiosity. The Bottle House is also listed on the National Register of Historic Places, giving the unusual structure recognition beyond the local community.A discarded bottle became part of historyWhat makes the Kaleva Bottle House remarkable is the simple idea behind it. Bottles that could no longer serve their original purpose were not simply thrown away. They became part of a building that has survived for generations. John Makinen's decision in 1941 transformed thousands of unwanted bottles into walls, patterns and eventually a landmark. When the Kaleva Historical Society bought the property in 1983, it preserved not only an unusual house but also a physical reminder of the ingenuity and history of the local community.Today, the bottles that once came from a Michigan bottling factory remain embedded in the walls, turning an unconventional building project into a lasting piece of Kaleva's history.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1963, Heineken made 50,000 World Bottles designed to double as building bricks; two years later a prototype glass house was built, but technical hurdles stopped the concept from reaching the market
articles.summary: In 1963, Heineken produced 50,000 rectangular bottles designed to work as both beer containers and building bricks.
articles.body: In 1963, Heineken produced 50,000 rectangular bottles designed to work as both beer containers and building bricks. The idea came from Alfred Heineken, who wanted the bottles to serve a second purpose after the beer had been consumed. Two years later, a prototype glass house was built using the unusual bottles, but the concept never reached the market because of technical and commercial problems.According to Smithsonian Magazine, the idea began with a trip to the Caribbean island of Curacao in 1960. Alfred Heineken noticed that Heineken bottles were scattered across the beaches. At the time, bottles were commonly returned to breweries for refilling and could make around 30 trips between consumers and breweries. But Curacao did not have enough infrastructure to collect and reuse all the bottles.At the same time, Heineken saw another problem. Some of the impoverished communities he visited had limited access to proper building materials. He began thinking about whether the same bottle causing a waste problem could also become part of a solution. That led to the idea of a 'brick that holds beer'.Back in the Netherlands, Heineken worked with architect John Habraken to develop the concept. The result was called the Heineken World Bottle, or WOBO. Unlike the company's familiar cylindrical beer bottle, the WOBO was rectangular and designed to be used as a building component after the beer was finished.How the bottle was designed The long sides of the WOBO had interlocking grooves. When the bottles were placed horizontally, these surfaces were intended to help them fit together and be stacked using mortar or cement. A small 10-foot-by-10-foot shack would have needed about 1,000 bottles to build.Yu Ren Guang described the thinking behind the design in Packaging Prototypes 3: Thinking Green- “On returning to Holland, Alfred set about conceiving the first ever bottle designed specifically for secondary use as a building component, thereby turning the function of packaging on its head,” Guang said as quoted by Smithsonian.The idea also attracted attention from designers. Martin Pawley described WOBO in Garbage Housing as “the first mass production container ever designed from the outset for secondary use as a building component.”But creating a bottle that could hold beer and also work as a brick was not simple. Several versions of the prototype were considered before the final design was produced.One major problem was the bottle's neck. A beer bottle needs a neck so that people can pour and drink from it. But that same protruding neck made the bottle harder to stack after use. A brick-shaped bottle therefore had to balance the requirements of a drinking container with those of a building material.The final WOBO design came in two sizes, 350 and 500 millimetres. The smaller bottle was intended to work as a half-brick, helping builders even out rows during construction. In 1963, Heineken produced 50,000 WOBO bottles for commercial use.Why the brick bottle never reached marketDespite the unusual design, the WOBO did not become a commercial beer bottle. The problems were not limited to its shape.The bottle had to be made with thicker glass because it was designed to be laid horizontally. That increased the cost of producing it. Conventional cylindrical bottles were cheaper and could also be produced faster.There was another issue. Customers were already familiar with cylindrical bottles and found them easy to hold. The rectangular WOBO changed that familiar experience.Earlier designs also faced criticism. Two models were ultimately rejected by Heineken. One prototype was described by the company's marketing team as too “effeminate” because of the shape of the bottle.Although the bottle did not enter the market, Heineken did build a working demonstration. In 1965, a prototype glass house was constructed near Alfred Heineken's villa in Noordwijk, outside Amsterdam.The project went beyond the bottles themselves. Plastic shipping pallets that had been intended for transporting the WOBOs were also reused as sheet roofing for the structure. The two buildings still stand at the former brewery site that is now the Heineken Experience museum.The idea continued beyond WOBOHeineken's failure to commercialise the brick bottle did not end the wider idea of designing bottles for secondary uses. Another company, EM1UM, later developed bottles that could be connected lengthways or sideways. Their designs used knobs and depressions that allowed the bottles to attach to one another.EM1UM's bottles were easier to manufacture using automatic bottling machines than the Heineken design and saw most of their success in Argentina. The company also received awards for bottle designs including prisms, cubes and cylinders.The WOBO idea was revisited again in 2008. French design company Petit Romain developed plans for a product called the Heineken Cube. Like the original WOBO, it was designed to be stackable and easier to pack than conventional cylindrical bottles. But unlike WOBO, the Cube was intended to save space during travel rather than become a building material. The Heineken Cube also remained a prototype.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Floodgates opened at 10 reservoirs as heavy rain raises river levels
articles.summary: Heavy rain in Jharkhand forces floodgates open at 10 reservoirs; Gonda and Getalsud release water as river levels rise near danger marks in Ranchi.
articles.body: Ranchi: Heavy rain triggered by a deep depression over the Bay of Bengal has pushed water levels in 10 of Jharkhand’s 62 reservoirs to their maximum thresholds, prompting authorities to open floodgates and regulate the inflow.Three of the reservoirs are in Gumla and three in Simdega, while Ranchi, West Singhbhum, Pakur and Lohardaga have one each.“Our teams are keeping a close watch on water levels at all reservoirs. Regulatory measures are being taken wherever the water approaches the maximum threshold, and locals in these areas have been alerted,” said Moti Lal Pingua, engineer-in-chief, water resources department.In Ranchi, one gate of Gonda dam has been open since Thursday after the water level crossed its maximum threshold of 2,128 feet. Rajesh Ranjan, executive engineer of the drinking water and sanitation department at Gonda dam, said the gate was opened to balance the inflow and outflow.“As of now, only one gate has been opened. If required, more gates will be opened,” he said.Two gates of Getalsud reservoir were opened as a precaution on Saturday morning after the water level reached 1,934.03 ft, against its maximum capacity of 1,936 ft. Hatia dam’s water level stood at 2,198.6 ft, just below its limit of 2,200 ft. No gates have been opened there so far.The reservoirs that crossed their capacity in Gumla are Paras, Dhansingtoli and Tapkara. In Simdega, the affected reservoirs are Larwa, Kansjor and Ramrekha. The others are Nandani in Lohardaga, Torlo in West Singhbhum and Suryodi in Pakur.Among the major rivers, Kharkai in Jamshedpur rose to 129.12 metres near Adityapur bridge, crossing its danger mark of 129 m. Subarnarekha reached 120.4 m near Mango bridge, close to its danger level of 121.5 m. Ajay and Sone rivers also recorded a rise but remained below their respective danger marks.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Madhubani Police identify 4 after old video of minor’s assault surfaces
articles.summary: Madhubani police identify four men after month-old viral video shows minor girl assaulted in field; FIR filed at Jaynagar, special team formed to arrest accused.
articles.body: Patna: Madhubani police have identified four men allegedly seen assaulting a minor girl in a video that surfaced on social media and have formed a special team to arrest the accused. An FIR is being registered at Jaynagar police station, police said on Saturday.The video came to the notice of the district police’s Social Media Cell during routine monitoring on Saturday. Taking cognisance of the footage, SP Yogendra Kumar directed SP (Rural) Shivam Dhakar and Jaynagar SDPO Sadanand Kumar to verify the incident and initiate legal action.During the inquiry, the SDPO visited the girl’s village and spoke to her family members and neighbours. Police said the video was recorded around a month ago and was not linked to any recent incident.According to the preliminary investigation, the girl and a neighbouring boy, with whom she was allegedly in a relationship, were found together in a field. Police said some villagers allegedly assaulted the girl in the presence of her family.Family members told police that later the same day, the girl married the boy. The marriage was reportedly conducted with the consent of family members and local residents. Police said the girl is currently living with her in-laws in Nepal.Police said the four men seen allegedly assaulting the girl in the viral video have been identified. articles.title: Four flights diverted, 26 delayed amid rain & gusty winds in Patna
articles.summary: Four flights were diverted and 26 delayed at Patna airport as heavy rain and gusty winds disrupted landings; one IndiGo Delhi–Patna–Delhi service was cancelled.
articles.body: Patna: Incessant rain and gusty winds disrupted flight operations at Jayprakash Narayan International Airport in Patna on Saturday with four flights diverted, 26 delayed and one cancelled, inconveniencing passengers and affecting subsequent services.IndiGo flight 6E-713 from Kolkata to Patna was diverted back to Kolkata after unsuccessful landing attempts. It landed in Kolkata at 1.10pm and later reached Patna at 4.56pm, against its scheduled arrival of 11.55am.IndiGo flight 6E-2373 from Delhi to Patna was diverted to Kolkata and reached Patna at 4.31pm, almost four hours behind schedule. Air India flight AI-2789 from Mumbai to Patna was diverted to Varanasi after several landing attempts and remained in the vicinity of Patna airport for almost two hours. It landed in Varanasi at 2.38pm and later reached Patna at 4.49pm.Air India Express flight IX-1510 from Delhi to Patna was also diverted to Varanasi before arriving in Patna at 5.25pm. The diversions and prolonged flight operations had a knock-on effect on other services.IndiGo flight 6E539 from Chennai to Patna remained in the vicinity of the airport for nearly an hour while attempting to land and made several go-arounds. Similar conditions affected five-six other flights.An ATC official said the diversions were prompted by bad weather and fluctuating winds. “Gusty conditions prevailed, with wind speed reaching around 25 knots, or about 46 kmph, at times. It would slow down and then pick up again, making landing conditions difficult,” the official said.According to airport data, 13 arrival and 13 departure flights were delayed. IndiGo’s Delhi-Patna-Delhi services 6E2482/6E6046 were cancelled.Patna Airport posted on X: “Indigo flight 6E-2482/6046 (Delhi-Patna-Delhi), scheduled to depart at 10.10pm from Patna, has been cancelled on Saturday, due to bad weather, as informed by the Indigo team (sic).”The disruption affected aircraft and crew rotations, leaving passengers waiting for extended periods.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news. articles.title: Three booked for Bengal truck driver’s death in Dhanbad
articles.summary: Police in Dhanbad booked three men for the death of Bengal truck driver Hasan Mandal after an alleged assault during sand loading; raids on absconding accused.
articles.body: Dhanbad: Police have intensified their investigation into the death of truck driver Hasan Mandal, 48, who allegedly succumbed to injuries sustained in an assault while loading sand at Polkera village in Dhanbad district.On Saturday, police registered an FIR against three residents of Polkera — Mannu Mandal alias Manu Mahto, Tarapad Mahto and Mangal Mahto — based on a complaint filed by Hasan’s brother, Taizul Mandal. He alleged that the accused attacked Hasan with sticks and iron rods, inflicting injuries that later proved fatal.Hasan, a resident of Bagdanga in West Bengal’s Nadia district, had reached Polkera around 10:30 pm on Wednesday along with truck cleaner Biswanath Das and owner Mafizul Malik. According to Biswanath, four to five men arrived and assaulted Hasan without any apparent provocation.Despite his injuries, Hasan managed to drive the truck for about half a km before losing consciousness. Biswanath then alerted sand stockist Sikandar Ansari, who reached the spot with others and took Hasan to a private hospital in Dhanbad. He died during treatment.On Friday, Taizul, Biswanath and Mafizul went to Nirsa police station. A police team led by Nirsa SDPO Lileshwar Mahto took them to Polkera, inspected the alleged crime scene, searched nearby areas and raided the homes of the three accused. However, all three are absconding.SP (rural) S Mohammad Yakub said a case had been registered and raids were under way to arrest the accused.Dhanbad mining inspector Shyam Mandal said illegal sand extraction was allegedly continuing in some areas with local support despite restrictions. He added that the department was taking steps to curb the practice.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. Download the TOI App.
